claims.text: The room-temperature HfNbTaTiZr alloy is a single-phase BCC solid solution.
The room-temperature HfNbTaTiZr alloy is chemically disordered.
Heating HfNbTaTiZr to approximately 600–1000°C induces short-range atomic ordering and local chemical clustering.
Elevated temperature provides sufficient atomic mobility for locally ordered clusters to form in the disordered BCC matrix.
Short-range ordered clusters alter local elastic anisotropy and elastic moduli through enhanced directional bonding.
Short-range ordered clusters alter dislocation mobility and dislocation-core structures.
Cluster formation may switch the dominant deformation mechanism, for example by favoring edge-dislocation activity or modifying slip behavior.
Elevated-temperature HfNbTaTiZr will exhibit temperature-dependent anisotropic changes in elastic moduli.
The alloy will show a reduced rate of thermal softening or anomalously maintained yield strength relative to room-temperature-based extrapolations.
The alloy's thermal expansion coefficient will differ from its lower-temperature behavior because of short-range ordering.
At room temperature, the alloy has a uniform isotropic elastic response and predictable thermal expansion behavior.
The proposed short-range-ordering mechanism should operate between approximately 600°C and 1000°C, before long-range diffusion or phase separation occurs.
Below 600°C conventional dislocation glide may dominate, while above 1000°C diffusion-induced coarsening may dominate.
In situ neutron diffraction can determine temperature-dependent elastic behavior and elastic moduli in a single-BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
The proposed test ramps HfNbTaTiZr from room temperature to 1100°C while collecting diffraction, mechanical, elastic, and lattice-expansion measurements.

The hypothesis is falsified if no diffraction signature of short-range ordering appears from 600°C to 1000°C and all measured responses follow ordinary uniform softening and expansion without anomalous mitigation.
